summary: categorically, and unequivocally rejected the Petitioner’s Change in Law claim. Both PTC and TNPDCL returned the supplementary invoices raised by the Petitioner not merely on the ground that no prior determination of the Commission had been obtained, but fundamentally because no Change in Law entitlement was ever admitted under the contractual framework; no Change in Law event was ever recognised or accepted by the Respondents; and the mandatory contractual preconditions under Articles 10.3.3 and 10.3.4 requiring prior determination of occurrence of the event as well as quantification of impact by the Appropriate Commission were never fulfilled. Accordingly, the Petitioner’s contention that the Respondents “did not dispute the occurrence of the event” is wholly fallacious and erroneous. (k) The Respondents’ insistence on prior adjudication by this Commission, as contemplated under Articles 10.3.3 and 10.3.4 of the PPA, cannot be mischaracterised as an admission of liability or acceptance of the Petitioner’s claims. This requirement is a mandatory contractual condition precedent, and the Respondents’ adherence to the same merely reflects compliance with the PPA mechanism. It does not imply that the Respondents accept either the occurrence of a Change in Law event or the Petitioner’s entitlement to any compensation thereunder. In light of the above, the Petitioner’s allegation that the Respondents did not dispute the occurrence of the alleged Change in Law event is wholly misconceived, factually untenable, and legally unsustainable. The said allegation is therefore liable to be rejected in limine. (l) This Commission, vide Order dated 29.1.2020, dismissed Petition No. 305/MP/2015 filed by the Petitioner in relation to its PPA with WBSEDCL, holding categorically that the cancellation of the Ganeshpur coal block does not constitute a Change in Law event. The Petitioner thereafter preferred an Appeal, and the APTEL, vide Order dated 4.9.2025, set aside the said decision and remanded the matter. It is pertinent that TNPDCL was not a party to those proceedings, nor was the TNPDCL PPA ever under consideration before either this Commission or the APTEL in that context. It is relevant to note that in the rejoinder filed by the Petitioner in Petition No. 305/MP/2015, the Petitioner expressly stated, in response to the reply filed by TNPDCL, that TNPDCL had been impleaded only for the limited purpose of demonstrating the composite scheme, and that no relief whatsoever was being claimed under the TNPDCL -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Order in Petition No. 845/MP/2025 Page 21 of 81 PPA. The Petitioner is misleadingly relying on APTEL’s judgment dated 4.9.2025 rendered exclusively in the context of the WBSEDCL PPA to persuade this Commission to issue directions of a computational nature in the present matter. The directions emanating from the APTEL judgment are inextricably linked to the adjudication of rights and obligations under the WBSEDCL PPA. Those directions arise solely in the proceedings remanded to this Commission in respect of that PPA. The APTEL judgment does not concern TNPDCL, does not adjudicate upon the TNPDCL PPA, and does not create any substantive or procedural rights in favour of the Petitioner under the TNPDCL contractual framework. (m) The Petitioner’s claim is fundamentally predicated on the Orders dated 20.4.2023 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the cases of GMR Warora and MSEDCL v. Adani Power. The Petitioner has expressly relied upon these judgments as the basis for filing the present Petition. However, even assuming, without admitting, that these judgments confer any benefit on similarly placed parties, the Petitioner cannot take advantage of them, having failed to assert or prosecute its rights diligently and at the appropriate time. The law is well settled that the mere fact that relief has been granted to another similarly placed party does not entitle a person who has slept over his rights to seek identical relief by filing belated proceedings. Nor does the subsequent success of another litigant stop or exclude the running of limitation, which begins from the date the cause of action first arises. It is a settled principle of law that parties who fail to pursue their remedies within the prescribed time cannot subsequently seek parity with those who acted diligently. Therefore, the Petitioner’s reliance on the order in GMR Warora and MSEDCL v. Adani Power is wholly misplaced. These judgments cannot resurrect a claim that is hopelessly barred by limitation, nor can they validate a cause of action that the Petitioner allowed to lapse through its own prolonged and inexplicable inaction. The Petition, a textbook example of fence-sitting, deserves dismissal on this ground alone. (n) In any event, no Change in Law arises in the instant case, since the Petitioner had full knowledge of and was fully aware of the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s ongoing scrutiny and eventual cancellation of captive coal blocks, including the Ganeshpur block; the Petitioner deliberately quoted a bid premised on linkage coal up to 30.11.2015 and captive coal from 1.12.2015 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Order in Petition No. 845/MP/2025 Page 22 of 81
title: Petition under Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Article 10 of Power Purchase Agreement dated 18.12.2013 (Procurers PPA) and Schedule I (VIII) of the Power Purchase Agreement dated 19.12.2013 (PTC PPA) seeking compensation/consequential reliefs on account of occurrence of Change in Law event impacting revenues and costs during operating period. Adhunik Power and Natural Resources Limited
